record.paper_title: The origin and evolution of transition discs: successes, problems and open questions
record.original_question: Do discs that retain a primordial-looking spectral energy distribution but show a large mm cavity constitute a hidden population physically associated with transition discs, and if so are they precursors to, contemporaries of, or descendants from the better-known transition-disc classes?

evidence.quote: Finally, we suggest that the few discs with primordial looking SEDs, but serendipitously imaged, showing large cavities in the mm (e.g. MWC758 & WSB 60) may represent a hidden population of associated objects.
Whether these are an isolated rare example or point to a large hidden population of discs with no NIR deficient and a mm hole is an intriguing question.

Characterising whether these disc are an a stage in the evolution of a transition disc: i.e. are they precursors or former transition discs would place further constraints on any transition disc models.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the study of circumstellar dust discs around young stellar objects, a "transition disc" is conventionally identified by a deficit of near- and/or mid-infrared excess in its spectral energy distribution (SED), interpreted as a depletion of small dust within an inner cavity. High-resolution millimetre interferometric imaging has, however, revealed objects (such as MWC 758 and WSB 60) whose SEDs look indistinguishable from those of "primordial" (full) discs — i.e. they show no near-infrared deficit — yet whose resolved millimetre continuum images exhibit a large central cavity in the large (mm-sized) dust grains.

Address the following questions:

(a) Do such objects (primordial-looking SED together with a resolved large mm-wavelength cavity in the large dust component) constitute a statistically significant hidden population among Class II circumstellar discs, rather than isolated peculiar cases?

(b) If such a population exists, determine whether it is physically related to the canonical transition-disc classes (those identified by infrared SED deficits and/or by resolved mm cavities accompanied by an SED deficit). Specifically, decide which of the following evolutionary relationships best describes them:
  (i) precursors that subsequently develop into infrared-deficient transition discs;
  (ii) contemporaneous counterparts representing a parallel manifestation of the same physical mechanism (e.g. dust filtration, planet-disc interaction, photoevaporation) but with differing small-dust content in the inner disc;
  (iii) descendants representing a later evolutionary stage of previously infrared-deficient transition discs after replenishment of small inner dust.

Provide observational and/or theoretical criteria (e.g. occurrence rates, accretion rates, stellar ages, inner-disc gas/small-dust content, scattered-light morphology) that would discriminate among (i)–(iii).
artifact.status_search_result: Recent observational campaigns (DSHARP, ODISEA, and follow-up ALMA surveys through 2023–2025) have continued to identify additional discs with primordial-like SEDs but resolved mm cavities (e.g. some "Peter Pan" and full-SED ringed discs), suggesting such systems are not unique. However, no consensus has been reached on whether they form a coherent hidden population or on their evolutionary relationship (precursor, contemporary, or descendant) to classical transition discs; the question remains an active open problem in disc evolution.

status_evidence.title: DSHARP and subsequent ALMA disc surveys
status_evidence.snippet: High-resolution ALMA imaging reveals substructures (rings, cavities) in many discs whose SEDs do not show classical transition-disc IR deficits.
status_evidence.claim: Discs with full SEDs but resolved mm substructures/cavities are commonly observed, but their evolutionary status relative to transition discs is unresolved.
